Ajay Shah recalls ERNET, once India’s only internet connection

brief.head: Two traps for thinkers
brief.text: The first barrier to changing your mind is conventional wisdom and famous names, Ajay Shah said, which he has resisted since childhood. The second, arrogance, he finds harder. {055-C01}

brief.head: Protection backfires
brief.text: Cutting customs duties makes imported inputs cheaper and exports more competitive, Ajay Shah said. The belief that exporting needs more protectionism is “trivially and factually wrong”. {055-C02}

brief.head: The alumni effect
brief.text: Foreign firms often lead, Ajay Shah said, and their alumni then build domestic firms. Bangladesh’s garment exports grew that way, as Indian software did from Datamatics and TCS. {055-C05}

brief.head: No applause for upkeep
brief.text: Politicians and officials enjoy announcements and inaugurations, Ajay Shah said. The quiet, humdrum work of running and regulating assets wins no applause, and is where the Indian state is weakest. {055-C08}

brief.head: Bid for the subsidy
brief.text: Ashok Lahiri’s viability gap funding, Ajay Shah said, lets bidders compete on how little subsidy they need for a road. The subsidy is then fixed, keeping the builder disciplined. {055-C10}

thought.text: When the facts change, I change my mind, and what do you do, sir?
thought.who: John Maynard Keynes’s line, held up by Ajay Shah as an ideal he reaches too slowly

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah question a development faith
lead.head: Fibre delivered, the ports didn’t
body: Since the 1990s, building roads, ports and airports has been treated in India as a sure bet for development. In this episode, Ajay Shah, who backed that bet, said it had come good only halfway.
Services exports, he told Amit Varma, had worked “beyond our wildest dreams”. The ports, highways, airports and railways built to move goods did not.
“IT today is India’s biggest industry. IT is what India does. IT is the only thing India has won in,” Shah said. {055-C06}
For goods, he said, “I just kept watching the data and hoping and watching the data and hoping.”
## The theory of the nineties
The theory came out of the 1990s, Shah explained. Customs duties fell, rules on foreign investment changed, and exports surged. Then the infrastructure choked.

Half or more of world trade, Shah said, happens inside firms, which put each stage of production wherever it is cheapest. “We have no interest in nationality,” he said. “We just care that production should be done in India.” {055-C03}

That meant moving intermediate goods cheaply to remote places where labour is cheap. So infrastructure climbed onto the “high table of development strategy”, Shah said, before catching himself anthropomorphising it.
## One success, one disappointment

For services, the theory worked. Once the state broke the telecom monopoly, private firms laid fibre optic cables into India, and services work spread from Bangalore and Hyderabad to dozens of smaller cities.

For goods, it did not. Shah took the ten years from 2012-13 to 2022-23, a window that flatters India because it includes the post-pandemic boom. Even then, goods exports grew 1.3 per cent a year in real dollars. {#real}

At that rate, he said, exports double every 52 or 56 years, “which is just nothing”. Foreign direct investment grew about 4 per cent a year in real terms. Global firms had not chosen India as a manufacturing platform.
## Less bang for the buck
Shah gave four reasons why each rupee of infrastructure now buys less, using a measure economists call the incremental capital output ratio, or ICOR.

The best projects, such as the Golden Quadrilateral and JNPT, were done first. {055-C07} The state retreated from public-private partnerships to building itself. Project choice turned political. And officials prefer launching projects to running them.
China, he said, had run into the same problems, building “roads to nowhere” and wasting trillions of dollars of poor people’s money.

Varma drew the lesson for public money. Every rupee the state spends, he noted from Shah’s book with Vijay Kelkar, *In Service of the Republic*, costs about three rupees of GDP, so spending needs strong reasons.

Shah linked the argument to the previous episode, on education. Lant Pritchett, he said, had been the little child saying the emperor has no clothes, showing that piling on years of schooling did not deliver development. The episode’s title echoes Pritchett’s paper.
The question that matters, Shah said, is what most holds back firms from producing across India. “Infrastructure is probably not the binding constraint today.” {055-C11}
That could change. If India fixed whatever deters foreign firms and investment poured in, jammed ports and roads would make infrastructure the choke point again.
Shah admitted that the conclusion cuts against his own past. “I was supporting that main paradigm in the nineties,” he said. “I’m just saying that my views have shifted.”

second.label: China’s build-out
second.head: The road less travelled
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how China’s infrastructure build wasted trillions
body: China’s infrastructure build was driven by central planners and optimistic economists who believed that more infrastructure would bring lots of good things, Ajay Shah said. Over time, political decisions took over, and roads were built with nothing at the other end. {055-S06}

In the short run, everyone was happy: there were construction contracts, announcements and ribbon cuttings. But measured as incremental investment against incremental GDP, each round bought less, and China’s ICOR kept getting worse.

By any reasonable account, Shah said, China built too much infrastructure and wasted trillions of dollars of the hard-won money of poor people. It is time, he argued, for India to ask whether it should keep on doing more and more. {#india}

quote.text: There’s nothing at the other end. But vast money would be spent.

second.caption: China’s roads to nowhere

third.head: Sweet, made in USA
body: Capitalism, Ajay Shah told Amit Varma, works by equalising differences: if wages, land or materials are cheaper somewhere, make the thing there and sell it where prices are high. {055-C04} Nobody in a good frame of mind, he said, would do low-end garment work in Bombay.
So you would never make chikki in Lonavala, where real estate is expensive. Was it made in China, Varma asked? Not China, Shah said, but Ulhasnagar. He had gone on a field trip to find out. {055-S08}
The punchline, Shah said, was the answer he got: “Of course we don’t make it here. We make it in Ulhasnagar.”
Varma had a label ready. “So you could actually write on it made in USA,” he said. “USA standing for Ulhasnagar Sweets Association.” {055-J02}
third.caption: the chikki of Ulhasnagar

p2.title: Where has it all gone?
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case, chapter by chapter, that India’s infrastructure bet worked for services and failed for goods

sections.label: The theory
sections.head: Make it where it’s cheap
sections.caption: why infrastructure mattered
body: The case for infrastructure, Ajay Shah said, begins in the 1990s. Customs duties came down, rules against foreign investment changed, and India got “a first surge of beautiful exports growth”. {055-C02}
Then the infrastructure choked, and it shot up everyone’s list of priorities.

The deeper reason lies in how global firms work. Half or more of global trade happens within firms. A ball bearing goes to Brazil, an engine is made there, the engine comes to Madras, and the car is made in Madras and shipped out. A country prospers, Shah said, by hosting such production chains, whether the firms are Indian or foreign. {055-C03}
## Equalising differences

Shah offered a trick for understanding the world: capitalism works by equalising differences. Any gap in wages, land or raw material costs is a business opportunity. You cannot house fourteen hundred million people in Bombay, he said, and its wages and real estate are too high for low-end garment work anyway. {#bombay}

So the plan was for firms to put factories in remote places where labour is cheap, and for roads, railways, ports and airports to carry the ball bearing in and the result out. That, Shah said, is how infrastructure became central to India’s growth strategy.
~ It was not his idea, he stressed. In the 1990s, he said, the best and brightest economists understood the whole story, and the dream was “sky high”.

quote.text: Capitalism works by equalising differences. So if there’s a difference in a wage there’s a business opportunity.

sections.label: The good story
sections.head: Getting out of the way
sections.caption: the telecom revolution
body: Telecom, Ajay Shah said, is “really a great success story”. In the late 1990s the Vajpayee government broke the Department of Telecom’s stranglehold on telecom policy and opened the sector to private and foreign investment. VSNL lost its monopoly on international telephony.

Private firms then ran fibre optic cables to India, with landing stations from the Middle East to Bombay and from Madras to Singapore. Users paid for it through their broadband bills. “You don’t need government money,” Shah said. “This should be about government getting out of the way.” {055-S02}
Amit Varma remembered the objections of the time: telecom was too important, national security was at stake, the state should control it. People forget those arguments today, he said.
## Eight years late

Shah’s one complaint is timing. The reforms should have come on the same day as the customs duty cuts, when India could import computer hardware and network switches. “We lost about eight years to get to ninety nine,” he said. {#eightyears}
By then, the ERNET project had already seeded hundreds of people with UNIX and internet knowledge, on a pittance of a budget. {055-S01}
~ IT-ITES is now India’s biggest industry, Shah said, with some three hundred to four hundred billion dollars a year of fast-growing services exports.

quote.text: So the full country was riding on 1.54 megabits a second.

sections.label: The bad story
sections.head: Watching and hoping
sections.caption: the goods that never took off
body: Ports, highways, airports and railways were meant to do for goods what fibre did for services. A factory in remote Vidarbha would make white cotton shirts and ship them to Europe. “But it didn’t work out,” Ajay Shah said.
Shah calls himself an enthusiast for India, and year after year he watched the export numbers. “I just kept watching the data and hoping and watching the data and hoping.” {055-S05}
## A window that flatters

To paint India at its best, he picked the ten years from 2012-13 to 2022-23. That window includes the surge in goods exports after the pandemic, when rich governments sent households big fiscal support. Goods exports grew 4 per cent a year in nominal dollars. {#goodsgrowth}
Taking out American inflation, about 2.7 per cent, left 1.3 per cent a year in real terms: a doubling every half-century or so. FDI grew at about 4 per cent a year in real terms.
Shah insisted on counting in constant US dollars, not rupees, since exchange rates and inflation can create a money illusion, and goods such as iron ore are priced in dollars anyway. {#measure}
~ Global firms, his conclusion ran, had not taken to India as a manufacturing platform. “It’s time to officially announce that the goods export story from India is not going well.”

quote.text: I’m an enthusiast for India. I just kept hoping that this will work.

sections.label: Diminishing returns
sections.head: Low-hanging fruit, all picked
sections.caption: the falling bang for the buck
body: Why does infrastructure now give less bang for the buck? Ajay Shah gave four reasons, measured by the incremental capital output ratio, or ICOR.

First, diminishing returns. The best projects, such as the Golden Quadrilateral, JNPT and the Delhi metro, get taken up first. {055-C07} “By the time you’re doing a metro in Nagpur, frankly, there’s very little use of a metro in Nagpur,” he said. {055-J04}

Second, after a “valiant and heroic attempt” at public-private partnerships from 1991 to 2011 went badly, the state retreated to building things itself, which costs more and is maintained worse. The right answer, Shah said, was to learn to contract better. {055-C09}
Third, project choice turns political: a powerful person’s constituency, a religious site, a marginal seat. Fourth, officials prefer ribbon cuttings to the humdrum work of running assets.
## Digging ditches

Amit Varma added Frédéric Bastiat’s lesson about the seen and the unseen. GDP counts state spending as output, he said, so “you could just have an army of people digging up ditches, filling them up”, and GDP would keep going up. {055-C12}
The real question, he said, is what the money would have done if left with the taxpayers it was taken from.
~ Varma’s own lesson, for individuals and institutions alike: don’t run away from hard problems just because they are hard.

quote.text: The right solution is not for a government to build stuff, but for a government to do complex contracts with private persons

sections.label: The core problem
sections.head: Find the choke point first
sections.caption: the binding constraint
body: There is no greater question for him, Ajay Shah said, than how India can put its pieces together and become an advanced economy.

He set this episode beside the previous one, on education. Lant Pritchett, in his paper *Where Has All the Education Gone?*, was “the little child saying that the emperor has no clothes”: years of schooling had been piled on without delivering development. {055-J09}
Shah mocked the old faith that schooling comparable to the UK of 1947 would make India like the UK of 1947. {055-J03} Money, he argued, should be pulled back until the failure is diagnosed.
## What holds firms back

Thinking on infrastructure, he said, may be at the early stages of the same scepticism. The central question in development economics is what most holds back firms, Indian or foreign, from locating production across India. “Infrastructure is probably not the binding constraint today.” {055-C11}

As a made-up example, he offered capital controls and hostile taxation. Make India as hospitable as an OECD country, and if a surge of FDI followed, full container ports and jammed roads would make infrastructure the constraint again.
~ “You must see those outcomes coming,” he added, “otherwise your theory is wrong.”

quote.text: You should not continue to put public money into things that are known to not work.

side.boxText: Lant Pritchett’s *Where Has All the Education Gone?* showed that piling on years of schooling did not deliver development. Ajay Shah now turns the same scepticism on infrastructure, and the episode borrows the paper’s question for its title. {055-R06}

contQuote.text: So the challenge of being a state is the challenge of high quality, quiet humdrum work where you don’t get applause and you don’t score propaganda points. And this is very difficult in the Indian state.

p3.title: Field notes
p3.deck: A factory, an internet line, a coast and a port, and what each teaches

stories.start: I visited a Blue Jeans manufacturing facility uh belonging to Irvine Mills in Bangalore
stories.end: hiring two thousand five hundred people from one factory on the outskirts of Bangalore
stories.caption: the jeans factory
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s two days on a Bangalore factory floor
stories.head: The robot that fades your jeans
body: A couple of months before the episode, Ajay Shah spent two days at a blue jeans factory belonging to Arvind, on the outskirts of Bangalore. He called them one of the greatest two days of his life.
The Arvind team had promised to show him one bad factory and one good one. The good one, they told him, was the best blue jeans factory in the country. “I take their word for it,” Shah said.
It is a single facility with about 2,500 blue-collar workers, and it exports everything it makes. {#jeans}

Inside, there is a constant march of machines. India’s minimum wages are high and benefits are mandatory, so to stay competitive with Bangladesh and Vietnam, the firm keeps adding machines one at a time, each justified by a hard-nosed internal rate of return calculation.
Even the work of making new jeans look old and faded is done by a robot. This, Shah said, is the “inefficient capital intensity” that microeconomics predicts.

Then there were the shifts. “In the day shift, it’s almost entirely women,” he said. Round the clock, problems of physical safety, transport and government regulation take over, “and then it’s 100% men.” {055-S07}

Amit Varma saw a classic illustration of how minimum wages harm the workers they are meant to help. Anyone whose work is valued below the minimum loses the job: “instead of earning X amount, they’re earning zero, and everybody would agree that zero is worse.” {055-C13}
~ Shah, who loves field visits, asked listeners to suggest more factories for him to visit.
stories.why: A factory floor shows how India’s labour rules shape firms. When the law makes workers expensive, even a labour-intensive industry like jeans turns to machines, and round-the-clock work becomes a job for men only.
stories.postscript: Varma recommended his episode with the economist Sowmya Dhanaraj, much of whose work is about women in factories.

stories.start: I remember when I first came back to India, there was only one source
stories.end: the seeding of the UNIX and internet knowledge all over the country
stories.caption: ERNET’s single line
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on India’s lone internet link of the early 1990s
stories.head: 1.54 megabits for all India
body: When Ajay Shah came back to India in the early 1990s, there was only one source of internet connectivity in the country: the National Centre for Software Technology, NCST.

Its head, S. Ramani, as Shah recalled, led a project called ERNET, a T1 line to the internet, which at the time sounded mind-blowing. {#t1} That meant 1.54 megabits a second for the whole of India. {055-S01}
On a pittance of a budget, ERNET seeded hundreds of people with UNIX and internet knowledge, including people the hosts know personally.

~ So when the telecom monopoly ended later in the decade, that knowledge had already spread across the country. “I really admire and I’m grateful to the people in ERNET who created that beginning,” Shah said.
stories.why: Small, well-placed spending on knowledge can matter enormously. ERNET built the human capital for the services boom before the bandwidth arrived, so that when private fibre came, people across India were ready to use it.

stories.start: I had a conversation with the founder of Emphasis, and he was saying
stories.end: So why will I build one more facility in Bangalore?
stories.caption: Mphasis on the coast
stories.kicker: A founder’s account of how services work spread
stories.head: Crawling up the coast
body: Services work did not stay in Bombay, Ajay Shah said. It went to Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune and Madras, and to dozens of smaller cities.

The founder of Mphasis once told him how. “Today we are crawling up the coast of Andhra Pradesh and Orissa,” the founder said, picking towns of five to ten lakh people: “we put a building there, we hire two thousand people there, and we are up and running.” {055-S03}

It starts with call centres, where the firm polishes recruits’ accent and grammar, and moves up to software. The worker stays close to her home instead of migrating, and fibre optic cables carry her work around the world.
~ This is equalising differences at work, Shah said: cheap labour in Vijayawada is cheaper than in Bangalore, so why build one more facility in Bangalore? {#vijayawada}

quote.text: Living close to her home, not needing to leave home and migrate.

stories.start: there was wonderful stuff done around pro competitive frameworks for the J NPT
stories.end: level of brilliance in policy doesn't happen in many later episodes in Indian infrastructure
stories.caption: JNPT’s three terminals
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a 1990s port design
stories.head: Competition docks at JNPT
body: In the 1990s, Ajay Shah said, there was wonderful work on pro-competitive frameworks for JNPT, then India’s biggest container terminal, in Bombay.
The government did not hand the port to one private operator as a single public-private partnership. Instead it organised JNPT as three competing terminals in one port. {055-S04}

One terminal stayed with the government, so that costs could be measured and prices benchmarked. The other two were contracted out to two different private vendors. The result, Shah said, was vigorous competition.

~ He counts JNPT, with the Golden Quadrilateral and the Bombay and Delhi airports, among the burning priorities of the 1990s: the projects with the highest bang for the buck, taken up first. {055-C07}

quote.text: Sadly some of that level of brilliance in policy doesn’t happen in many later episodes in Indian infrastructure.

quiz.q: On what single line did ERNET connect the whole of India to the internet in the early 1990s?
quiz.a: A T1 line, running at 1.54 megabits a second, for the full country.

quiz.q: Lonavala sells the chikki, but where did Ajay Shah’s field trip find it is made?
quiz.a: In Ulhasnagar. Lonavala real estate is expensive, so production moves somewhere cheaper.

quiz.q: Which ratio did Ajay Shah use to show infrastructure’s falling bang for the buck?
quiz.a: ICOR, the incremental capital output ratio, comparing extra capital with extra output.

quiz.q: How did the government design JNPT so that one port would have real competition?
quiz.a: As three competing terminals: one government-run, two contracted to different private vendors.

quiz.q: In Ashok Lahiri’s viability gap funding, what do bidders compete over in the reverse auction?
quiz.a: How little subsidy they need; the subsidy is then fixed for the builder.

quiz.q: Which economist’s line about changing your mind when facts change did Ajay Shah hold up?
quiz.a: John Maynard Keynes’s; Shah admitted he himself changes his mind too slowly.
